title: PKCS #1: RSA Cryptography Specifications Version 2.2
summary: This informational document republishes PKCS #1 version 2.2 from RSA Laboratories, with recommendations for implementing RSA public-key cryptography. It covers cryptographic primitives, encryption schemes, signature schemes with appendix, and ASN.1 syntax for keys and schemes.

plainLanguage.summary: RSA is a way to lock messages with a public key that anyone can use and a private key only you hold. This is the detailed instruction manual for doing it correctly.

subtitle: The reference recipe for RSA encryption and signatures: keys, padding schemes and the math underneath.

tldr.problem: Raw RSA is just modular exponentiation on integers. Real systems need agreed ways to turn messages into integers, pad them safely, and encode keys so that implementations interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: PKCS #1 v2.2 defines RSA key types, conversion and exponentiation primitives, two encryption schemes (RSAES-OAEP and RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5), two signature schemes with appendix (RSASSA-PSS and RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5), and ASN.1 syntax for keys and schemes.
tldr.outcome: It republishes PKCS #1 v2.2 from RSA Laboratories and moves change control to the IETF. It obsoletes RFC 3447. RSAES-OAEP and RSASSA-PSS are required for new applications; the v1.5 schemes remain for compatibility.

today: RFC 8017 is an Informational document that obsoletes RFC 3447. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the unit metadata, so it is the IETF's published form of PKCS #1 v2.2.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 8017 gives recommendations for implementing public-key cryptography based on the RSA algorithm. It covers four things: cryptographic primitives, encryption schemes, signature schemes with appendix, and ASN.1 syntax for representing keys and identifying the schemes.

The document is a republication of PKCS #1 v2.2 from RSA Laboratories' Public-Key Cryptography Standards series. By publishing it as an RFC, change control is transferred to the IETF, and it obsoletes RFC 3447. The recommendations are intended to be compatible with IEEE 1363, IEEE 1363a and ANSI X9.44, and they leave room for application standards to add constraints.

The schemes only process data with an RSA key. They do not say how to obtain or validate a key, so an application normally adds its own key management around them.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a rulebook for using RSA locks properly. It says how to build the lock and how to use it, but not how to hand out the keys.

sections.title: RSA Keys
sections.content:
An RSA public key is a pair (n, e): the modulus n and the public exponent e. In a valid key, n is the product of u distinct odd primes with u >= 2, and e is an integer between 3 and n - 1 that shares no factor with λ(n).

A private key has two allowed forms. The first is the pair (n, d). The second is a quintuple (p, q, dP, dQ, qInv) plus a possibly empty list of triplets (r_i, d_i, t_i) for extra primes, which lets the Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT) speed up private-key operations.

The specification supports multi-prime RSA, where the modulus has more than two prime factors. The stated benefit is lower computational cost for decryption and signing when the CRT is used, especially on multiprocessor platforms where the exponentiations can run in parallel.
sections.plainLanguage: The public key is the lock everybody can see, built from a big number. The private key is the secret way that number was made, and it lets only you open the lock.

sections.title: Conversion and Cryptographic Primitives
sections.content:
Two data conversion primitives move between octet strings and integers: I2OSP turns a nonnegative integer into an octet string of a given length, and OS2IP does the reverse. The first octet is the most significant.

Four cryptographic primitives do the math. RSAEP computes c = m^e mod n and RSADP computes m = c^d mod n. RSASP1 and RSAVP1 do the same operations for signing and verifying, and differ from the encryption pair only in the names of their arguments, because they serve different purposes. Each one rejects inputs that are not between 0 and n - 1.

The RFC stresses that primitives are building blocks and are not intended to provide security apart from a scheme.
sections.plainLanguage: The primitives are the raw gears: turn your message into a number, scramble it with the key, turn it back. On their own they are not safe, so they get wrapped in schemes.

sections.title: Encryption Schemes
sections.content:
An encryption scheme combines a message encoding step with the RSA primitives. Two are specified. RSAES-OAEP is REQUIRED to be supported for new applications. RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5 is included only for compatibility with existing applications.

RSAES-OAEP can encrypt messages up to k - 2hLen - 2 octets, where k is the modulus length in octets and hLen is the hash output length. It builds a data block from a hash of an optional label, zero padding, a 0x01 octet and the message, then masks it with a mask generation function and a random seed. Under stated assumptions it is semantically secure against adaptive chosen-ciphertext attacks, although the RFC notes the security reduction is not efficient for concrete parameters.

RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5 handles messages up to k - 11 octets and encodes them as 0x00 || 0x02 || PS || 0x00 || M, with at least eight nonzero random padding octets. Valid ciphertexts can be generated without knowing the plaintext, which enables Bleichenbacher's chosen-ciphertext attack, so countermeasures are needed. Using it to encrypt arbitrary messages, as opposed to a randomly generated key, is NOT RECOMMENDED.

In both schemes, an attacker must not be able to tell the different decoding errors apart, whether by error message or by timing. Otherwise information about the decryption leaks.
sections.plainLanguage: OAEP is a tamper-proof envelope filled with random padding. The older v1.5 envelope has weaknesses, so it is kept only so old programs still work.

sections.title: Signature Schemes and Encoding
sections.content:
A signature scheme with appendix needs the message itself to verify the signature. Two are specified: RSASSA-PSS, REQUIRED in new applications, and RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5, kept for compatibility. The RFC says no attacks are known against the latter but recommends a gradual transition to PSS as a precaution.

EMSA-PSS is randomized. It hashes the message, mixes in a random salt, and masks the result, ending with a fixed trailer octet 0xbc. Its security can be tied closely to the difficulty of inverting RSA. The salt is not critical to security: where random generation is not possible, a fixed value or sequence number can be used. Typical salt lengths are hLen and 0.

EMSA-PKCS1-v1_5 is deterministic. It wraps the hash and the hash algorithm identifier as a DER-encoded DigestInfo and builds 0x00 || 0x01 || PS || 0x00 || T, where PS is 0xff octets, at least 8 of them. The RFC also advises using a given RSA key pair in only one scheme.
sections.plainLanguage: Signing is like stamping a document with a seal only you own. PSS adds a random swirl to each stamp so forgers have a harder time; the older method makes the same stamp every time.

sections.title: Hashes, Revisions and Security Notes
sections.content:
Appendix B lists nine example hash functions: MD2, MD5, SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512, SHA-512/224 and SHA-512/256. For new applications only the SHA-2 variants are RECOMMENDED. MD2 and MD5 are described as cryptographically broken and supported only for backwards compatibility, SHA-1 is recommended only for compatibility, and MD4 is NOT RECOMMENDED. The mask generation function defined is MGF1, which builds a mask by hashing a seed with a 4-octet counter.

The revision history shows how the standard grew. Version 2.0 introduced RSAES-OAEP, version 2.1 introduced multi-prime RSA and RSASSA-PSS, and version 2.2 added SHA-224, SHA-512/224 and SHA-512/256 to align with FIPS 180-4.

Section 10 on security considerations is one sentence: security considerations are discussed throughout the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: Some of the scrambling tools have gotten old and cracked, so the manual says which ones are still safe to pick and tells the story of how the manual grew.

data.title: Encoded message formats
data.code:
RSAES-OAEP:         EM = 0x00 || maskedSeed || maskedDB
RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5:   EM = 0x00 || 0x02 || PS || 0x00 || M
EMSA-PSS:           EM = maskedDB || H || 0xbc
EMSA-PKCS1-v1_5:    EM = 0x00 || 0x01 || PS || 0x00 || T
